\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{غرق} (ghariqa)}{غرق (ghariqa)}]{\ar{غرق} (ghariqa) — to go under; to drown}

\label{lesson:AR-C333-ghariqa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to be displaced, then the Arabic for to bid farewell.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{غرق}}
\textbf{\ar{غرق}} — \emph{ghariqa} — \textquotedblleft{}to go under; to drown\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{غرقت} \ar{السفينة} \ar{قرب} \ar{الجزيرة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ghariqat as-safīna qurba al-jazīra.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The ship sank near the island.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يغرق}, \emph{yaghraq}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{غرق}} (\emph{ghariqa}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{gh-r-q} (Lane), \textquotedblleft{}to sink in water, to drown\textquotedblright{}; \emph{gharīq} is one who has drowned.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ghariqa}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ghariqa}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ghariqat as-safīna qurba al-jazīra.} — The ship sank near the island.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to be displaced, then the Arabic for to bid farewell, then say \emph{ghariqa} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{غرق} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To go under; to drown\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{بحار} (baḥḥār)}{بحار (baḥḥār)}]{\ar{بحار} (baḥḥār) — a sailor}

\label{lesson:AR-C333-bahhar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to bid farewell, then the Arabic for to go under.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{بحار}}
\textbf{\ar{بحار}} — \emph{baḥḥār} — \textquotedblleft{}a sailor\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{عمل} \ar{جدي} \ar{بحارا} \ar{ثلاثين} \ar{سنة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ʿamila jaddī baḥḥāran thalāthīn sana.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My grandfather worked as a sailor for thirty years.
\end{quote}

Plural: \ar{بحارة}, \emph{baḥḥāra}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{بحار}} (\emph{baḥḥār}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{b-ḥ-r} (Lane), the root of the taught \emph{baḥr}, the sea. The \emph{faʿʿāl} pattern names a trade: \textquotedblleft{}the man of the sea\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{أسطول} (usṭūl)}{أسطول (usṭūl)}]{\ar{أسطول} (usṭūl) — a fleet}

\label{lesson:AR-C333-ustul}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to go under, then the Arabic for a sailor.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{أسطول}}
\textbf{\ar{أسطول}} — \emph{usṭūl} — \textquotedblleft{}a fleet\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{أرسل} \ar{الملك} \ar{أسطولا} \ar{إلى} \ar{الجزيرة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{arsala al-malik usṭūlan ilā al-jazīra.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The king sent a fleet to the island.
\end{quote}

Plural: \ar{أساطيل}, \emph{asāṭīl}.

Also a fleet of buses or lorries.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{أسطول}} (\emph{usṭūl}) is usually traced to Greek \emph{stolos}, \textquotedblleft{}an expedition, a fleet\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{قرصان} (qurṣān)}{قرصان (qurṣān)}]{\ar{قرصان} (qurṣān) — a pirate}

\label{lesson:AR-C333-qursan}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a sailor, then the Arabic for a fleet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{قرصان}}
\textbf{\ar{قرصان}} — \emph{qurṣān} — \textquotedblleft{}a pirate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{كان} \ar{القرصان} \ar{يبحث} \ar{عن} \ar{الكنز}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{kāna al-qurṣān yabḥathu ʿan al-kanz.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The pirate was looking for the treasure.
\end{quote}

Plural: \ar{قراصنة}, \emph{qarāṣina}.

Today also a computer hacker: \ar{قرصان} \ar{إنترنت}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{قرصان}} (\emph{qurṣān}) is usually traced to Italian \emph{corsaro}, \textquotedblleft{}a corsair\textquotedblright{}, the raider of the Mediterranean, from Latin \emph{cursus}, a running.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{أسر} (asara)}{أسر (asara)}]{\ar{أسر} (asara) — to capture, to take prisoner}

\label{lesson:AR-C333-asara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a fleet, then the Arabic for a pirate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{أسر}}
\textbf{\ar{أسر}} — \emph{asara} — \textquotedblleft{}to capture, to take prisoner\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{أسر} \ar{القراصنة} \ar{البحارة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{asara al-qarāṣina al-baḥḥāra.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The pirates took the sailors prisoner.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يأسر}, \emph{yaʾsir}.

A prisoner of war is \ar{أسير}. Of beauty: \ar{أسر} \ar{قلبه}, it captivated him.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{أسر}} (\emph{asara}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ʾ-s-r} (Lane), \textquotedblleft{}to bind with a thong\textquotedblright{}. Lane links the taught \emph{usra}, a family, to it: the kin who bind a man and stand with him.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{asara}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{asara}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{asara al-qarāṣina al-baḥḥāra.} — The pirates took the sailors prisoner.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for a fleet, then the Arabic for a pirate, then say \emph{asara} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{أسر} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To capture, to take prisoner\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
